clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive; most cases are due to biallelic CDAN1 variants encoding codanin-1, with a minority due to CDIN1 (C15orf41).
Presents with macrocytic anaemia and a reticulocyte response that is inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia, reflecting ineffective erythropoiesis.
The bone marrow shows megaloblastoid erythroid precursors with internuclear chromatin bridges between adjacent nuclei.
Electron microscopy reveals the characteristic spongy, 'Swiss-cheese' appearance of erythroblast heterochromatin.
Distal limb and skeletal anomalies such as syndactyly and nail changes may accompany the anaemia.
Iron overload develops even in the absence of regular transfusion and mandates surveillance and chelation.
The anaemia is frequently responsive to interferon-alpha, a feature that helps separate it from CDA type II.
May present in the neonatal period, occasionally with hydrops requiring intrauterine or early transfusion.
reference.pathophysiology: CDA type I is usually caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in CDAN1, encoding codanin-1, a negative regulator of the histone chaperone ASF1 and thus of nucleosome and chromatin assembly during DNA replication; a smaller subset results from variants in CDIN1 (C15orf41), whose product interacts with codanin-1 and is a putative nuclease. Disturbed chromatin condensation in erythroblasts produces the hallmark internuclear bridges and spongy heterochromatin, driving ineffective erythropoiesis with intramedullary destruction of abnormal precursors, macrocytic anaemia and inappropriate iron loading through suppressed hepcidin.
additionalDifferentials: Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with light microscopy for internuclear bridges
Molecular testing of CDAN1 and CDIN1
Exclusion of haemolysis and haematinic deficiency
redFlags: Complications of iron overload affecting the heart, liver or endocrine organs
Severe neonatal anaemia or hydrops fetalis
Symptomatic gallstones from chronic low-grade haemolysis
reference.prognosis: Anaemia is usually mild to moderate and often interferon-responsive, so long-term morbidity is driven mainly by iron overload; life expectancy is near normal with appropriate monitoring and chelation.
pitfalls: Iron overload accumulates despite the absence of transfusion and is easily overlooked.
The picture may be mistaken for a thalassaemia syndrome.
Interferon responsiveness helps distinguish it from CDA type II.
Haematinic deficiency should be excluded before attributing macrocytosis to the underlying CDA.
references: Red cell disorder and anaemia guidelines
management: Offer interferon-alpha therapy, to which type I anaemia is often responsive, reducing transfusion requirement
Treat iron overload with iron chelation therapy guided by ferritin and organ iron assessment, since loading occurs even without regular transfusion
Provide red cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia while minimising further iron loading
Supplement folic acid to support chronic erythropoiesis
Surveil for pigment gallstones and undertake cholecystectomy if symptomatic
Recognise and manage associated skeletal and distal limb anomalies such as syndactyly and nail changes
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive CDAN1 and CDIN1 inheritance, with haematology follow-up
